design_detail: Phase 1 double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled crossover in healthy volunteers at a Swiss university hospital, with three 10-hour dosing sessions at least 28 days apart in counterbalanced order: 120 mg MDMA followed two hours later by a 60 mg booster; 120 mg MDMA followed by placebo; and placebo followed by placebo. The primary outcome was the duration of any subjective drug effect, defined as the cumulative time a visual analogue rating of 'any drug effect' stayed above 10%. Secondary outcomes were other subjective ratings and mood, adverse effects by a 50-item complaint list at the end of the session and at 3 and 7 days, well-being and insomnia questionnaires, blood pressure, heart rate, rate-pressure product and temperature, and plasma concentrations of MDMA, MDA, HMMA, oxytocin and neurophysin I. Repeated-measures analyses of variance with Tukey post-hoc tests; registered as NCT05809271.
can_establish: Whether a 60 mg booster two hours after 120 mg MDMA, the regimen used in most MDMA-assisted-therapy trials, lengthens the acute response, raises its peak, changes plasma concentrations, or adds adverse effects, in the same healthy people against their own single-dose and placebo sessions.
cannot_establish: Whether a booster helps anyone therapeutically (no patients and no clinical outcome); what happens after more than two doses, at other intervals, or in people with hypertension or other illness; and whether the unchanged peak effects reflect tolerance rather than a ceiling on the rating scales, since no concentration-effect model is fitted and the hysteresis analysis that illustrates acute tolerance is in a supplement this reader did not open.

sample.recruitment: Volunteers recruited through the trial registry, advertisement and word of mouth, at the University Hospital Basel; study run between 17 November 2023 and 25 March 2025 (Methods > Study design; Results > Participants and blinding).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy adults aged 18-65 with a body mass index of 18-29. Excluded: pregnancy or breastfeeding, any past or current major psychiatric disorder by a structured DSM-5-based interview, a first-degree relative with a psychotic disorder, medication that could interact with MDMA, chronic or acute physical illness, smoking more than 10 cigarettes a day, drinking more than 15 standard drinks a week, lifetime MDMA use on more than 20 occasions, and any illicit drug use except cannabis within 2 months. Urine drug testing at screening and once during the study.
sample.demographics: Twenty-three completers (12 men, 11 women), mean age 35 years (SD 13), mean body weight 67 kg (SD 12). Ten (43%) had used MDMA before, on average 5.3 times (SD 3.8). Fuller baseline characteristics are in a supplementary table that was not read for this card.
sample.attrition: Two of 25 dropped out after their first session; both were women, both had received the booster condition as their first session and first ever MDMA experience, and both had intense headache and nausea during the session followed by weeks of anxiety, restlessness and impaired concentration, one with reduced ability to work for several months. Their complaint scores are reported separately and are excluded from the within-person comparisons.
sample.selection_effects: Healthy, mostly young volunteers screened to exclude psychiatric history, illness and heavy drug use, with little MDMA experience; the authors name the lack of generalizability to patients, particularly those with hypertension or other conditions, as a limitation. Because the two people with the worst reactions left after one session, the within-person comparisons of adverse effects are made among those who tolerated the drug.

exposure.measurement: Drug given in the hospital and measured directly: plasma MDMA, MDA and HMMA every 30 minutes for 6 hours and hourly thereafter by a validated method, with non-compartmental pharmacokinetics.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: oral racemic MDMA hydrochloride in 20 mg capsules made to Good Manufacturing Practice, measured content 20.74 mg (SD 0.47, n=10), with mannitol placebo capsules. The first dose was given at about 9 a.m. and the second exactly two hours later: 120 mg then 60 mg, 120 mg then placebo, or placebo then placebo.
exposure.polysubstance: Heavy drinking and smoking were exclusions, illicit drug use other than cannabis within two months was an exclusion, participants were asked to abstain during the study period and urine drug testing was done at screening and once during the study.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 28 days between sessions; sessions began after an overnight stay at home, with a standardized breakfast before the first dose. No breath or urine result is reported per session beyond the single in-study test.

comparison.controls: The same people in a placebo-placebo session and in a single-dose session; the booster condition is compared with both.
comparison.matching: Within-person, randomized and counterbalanced crossover with washout of at least 28 days.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable: every comparison is within person.

outcomes.instruments: Single-item 100 mm visual analogue scales, unidirectional (any drug effect, good drug effect, bad drug effect, drug liking, stimulated, drug high, anxiety) and bidirectional (emotional, talkative, happy, open, trust, close to others, wanting to be alone or with others), with 'any', 'good' and 'bad' drug effect every 15 minutes and the rest at 16 time points to 9 hours; the Adjective Mood Rating Scale at 5 time points; a 50-item List of Complaints at baseline, end of session and 3 and 7 days; the General Health Questionnaire-12, the Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-Being Scale and the Insomnia Severity Index at baseline and 3 and 7 days; blood pressure, heart rate, rate-pressure product and tympanic temperature; plasma MDMA, MDA, HMMA, oxytocin and neurophysin I.
outcomes.validity_norms: Validated instruments with published German versions and ranges given for each; the visual analogue scales are this group's standard measures with no external norms.
outcomes.operationalization: Effect duration is operationalized as the cumulative time the 'any drug effect' rating stays above 10%; acute tolerance is operationalized as effects subsiding while concentrations remain high, illustrated in a supplementary hysteresis plot rather than tested.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: One primary endpoint is declared (duration of any drug effect) and the rest are secondary; within each analysis, three conditions are compared by repeated-measures analysis of variance with Tukey post-hoc tests, but there is no correction across the many secondary outcomes.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind, with participants knowing the three conditions but not the order, and blinding kept to the end-of-study visit. Blinding was measured and largely failed for the drug itself: every participant identified the placebo condition correctly, and 35 of 46 MDMA conditions (76%) were identified correctly straight after the session, rising to 40 of 46 (87%) by the end of the study.

analysis.effect_sizes: Means with standard deviations for every subjective and adverse-effect outcome, F values with 2 and 44 degrees of freedom (consistent with 23 participants and three conditions) and post-hoc significance markers. Primary outcome: duration 5.6 h (SD 1.8) with the booster against 4.6 h (SD 1.5) with the single dose and 0.2 h (SD 0.5) with placebo (F=173, p<0.001; booster against single dose p<0.01). Peak 'any drug effect' 83 (SD 21) against 85 (SD 20), not significant, with the area under the effect curve 318 (SD 127) against 255 (SD 130), p<0.05. Peak 'good drug effect' 86 (SD 29) against 87 (SD 19), not significant. Pharmacokinetics as geometric means with ratios: peak MDMA concentration 387 ng/mL (95% CI 351-426) with the booster against 253 (228-280) with the single dose, ratio 1.50 (90% CI 1.43-1.57); exposure to 9 hours 2339 against 1564 ng.h/mL, ratio 1.47 (1.40-1.54); half-life 7.2 h in both; time to peak 4 h against 2.8 h. A sample size of 20 was calculated for 80% power to detect a within-person effect of about 0.66.
analysis.covariates: None; within-person analyses of variance. Exploratory descriptive stratification by sex, body weight (under or at least 65 kg) and age.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Registered at ClinicalTrials.gov as NCT05809271; the paper names the primary endpoint as the duration of the 'any drug effect' rating and reports it first. The registry record itself was not opened for this card, so the registered outcome could not be compared with the reported one.
analysis.selective_reporting: Much of the detail sits in supplementary tables and figures (baseline characteristics, blinding, the full subjective-effects table, mood ratings, the hysteresis plot illustrating acute tolerance, autonomic effects, oxytocin values, symptom frequencies, the stratified complaint scores, the two dropouts' scores and laboratory results); the main text reports autonomic effects only in words. This reader did not open the supplement, so those values are not in this card.
analysis.power: Prospective calculation: 20 participants for 80% power to detect a within-person difference of about 0.66 at a two-sided 5% level; 23 completed. The study is powered for its primary endpoint, not for the adverse-effect comparisons, where the authors report differences as nominally higher after the booster without reaching significance.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A 60 mg booster two hours after 120 mg lengthened the subjective effect by about an hour (5.6 against 4.6 hours) and raised the area under the effect curve for several ratings, while leaving peak ratings unchanged, even though peak plasma concentration and 9-hour exposure were about 1.5 times those of the single dose. Blood pressure, heart rate and temperature were likewise prolonged but not raised at the peak; oxytocin was higher at 4 and 6 hours. Acute and 3-day adverse-effect scores were higher after both MDMA conditions than placebo and did not differ between them, with complaint scores nominally but not significantly higher after the booster.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that acute MDMA effects can be prolonged by a booster, as intended in therapy trials, and that whether this translates into clinical benefit remains to be investigated: an unusually disciplined statement. The discussion reads the unchanged peaks against higher concentrations as acute pharmacodynamic tolerance. That reading is reasonable and consistent with the hysteresis plot the paper cites, but the peak ratings were already at 83-87 out of 100, so a ceiling on the scales cannot be separated from tolerance in these data; the paper does not raise that alternative for the subjective peaks, although it applies the same logic to the autonomic measures where no ceiling applies. The statement that the regimen was overall well tolerated sits beside two people, both women receiving the booster as a first MDMA experience, who left with weeks of psychological symptoms.

timeline.event: Two 100 mg doses 24 hours apart: exposure 77% higher after the second dose with several responses unchanged
Fifty mg then 100 mg two hours apart: concentrations above dose proportionality, heart rate and wanted effects not raised
Two 100 mg doses 4 hours apart (Farre et al., 2015): peak concentrations doubled while the two effect-time profiles were very similar

replication.where_it_stands: This is the first direct test of the booster regimen used in MDMA-assisted-therapy trials. Its central observation, effects that do not rise with concentration after a second dose, agrees with three earlier Spanish studies at other intervals; the new findings are the prolongation of about an hour and the absence of any added peak effect or clear added harm.

funding.funder: Swiss National Science Foundation grant 32003B_185111 to the senior author, the University Hospital Basel, and Lykos Therapeutics, Inc. (Funding statement).
funding.declared_conflicts: The senior author is a consultant for Mind Medicine, Inc. and Lykos Therapeutics, Inc.; the other authors declare none. After the study finished, University Hospital Basel granted Lykos Therapeutics the right to use the data to support regulatory submissions, and the paper states that Lykos had no role in planning or conducting the study or writing the manuscript.
funding.affiliations_note: University Hospital Basel and University of Basel. A company developing MDMA as a medicine part-funded the study and holds rights to the data for regulatory use, and the question studied, whether the booster dose in its trial regimen is justified, bears on that development. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A trial in patients receiving MDMA-assisted therapy, randomized to the booster or to a matched placebo booster, with the clinical outcome as the endpoint, so that the extra hour of acute effect can be weighed against any added harm; and, for the tolerance question, a design with scales that do not reach ceiling and a fitted concentration-effect model.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the three sessions)
domains.note: Order was randomized and counterbalanced and randomization, packaging and labelling were done by the manufacturer, but the sequence-generation method and concealment are not described in the main text and no period effect is reported.
At least 28 days between sessions, far beyond the 7.2-hour half-life.

Blinding was measured and largely failed: all participants identified placebo correctly and 76% of MDMA sessions were identified correctly immediately afterwards. The primary outcome is a self-rating of drug effect, so expectancy cannot be excluded, although the comparison of interest (booster against single dose) is between two conditions both felt as active.

Two of 25 left after one session and are excluded from within-person comparisons; both had the booster and both had strong adverse reactions, so the adverse-effect comparison is biased toward tolerability. Pharmacokinetic analyses retain them (n=25 for the booster, 23 for the single dose), and half-life rests on 15-16 profiles.

Plasma concentrations, oxytocin, blood pressure, heart rate and temperature are objective and measured with validated methods; the primary outcome is self-rated on an unblindable scale, and its threshold (10% of the scale) is a convention rather than a validated cut-off.

Registered in advance with a declared primary endpoint reported first, a prospective power calculation, and both positive and negative findings, serious adverse events and dropouts reported in detail.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: This is the best-designed of the repeated-dose MDMA studies read here: registered, powered, counterbalanced, with 28-day washouts, objective pharmacokinetics and full reporting of adverse events, including two dropouts that a less careful paper would have left out. The overall judgment is set by blinding, which the authors themselves measured and found largely broken, in a study whose primary outcome is a self-rating; the dropout pattern also leaves the tolerability comparison favourable by construction. The source can be cited for the booster's effect on duration, peak effects, concentrations, oxytocin and adverse effects in healthy volunteers, and for the observation that peak effects did not rise with 1.5-fold higher concentrations; it cannot be cited for clinical benefit, for patients, or for the size of acute tolerance.

key_findings.finding: The booster lengthened the subjective effect by about an hour: duration of 'any drug effect' above the 10% threshold was 5.6 h (SD 1.8) with the booster, 4.6 h (SD 1.5) with the single 120 mg dose and 0.2 h (SD 0.5) with placebo (F(2,44)=173, p<0.001; booster against single dose p<0.01).
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute subjective effects, 1st paragraph; Table 1, 'Any drug effect' duration row
key_findings.note: The abstract gives the single-dose standard deviation as 1.2 h and Table 1 as 1.5 h.

key_findings.finding: Peak subjective intensity did not rise with the booster: peak 'any drug effect' 83 (SD 21) against 85 (SD 20) and peak 'good drug effect' 86 (SD 29) against 87 (SD 19), neither significant, while the areas under the effect curves were larger with the booster for 'any drug effect' (318, SD 127, against 255, SD 130; p<0.05) and for openness, trust, talkativeness and wanting to be with others.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Emax and AUEC rows; Results > Acute subjective effects, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Plasma concentrations rose in proportion to the total dose: peak MDMA 387 ng/mL (95% CI 351-426) with the booster against 253 (228-280) with the single dose, a geometric mean ratio of 1.50 (90% CI 1.43-1.57); exposure to 9 hours 2339 against 1564 ng.h/mL, ratio 1.47 (1.40-1.54); elimination half-life 7.2 h in both conditions; time to peak 4 h against 2.8 h.

The authors read the combination of 1.5-fold higher concentrations with unchanged peak effects as acute pharmacodynamic tolerance, noting that subjective and physiological effects had subsided within the 9-hour observation while concentrations remained high, with the mean concentration at discharge after the booster exceeding the mean peak after the single dose.
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute subjective effects, last sentence; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The hysteresis plot said to illustrate this is in Supplementary Figure S2, which was not read for this card.

key_findings.finding: Autonomic effects followed the same pattern: blood pressure, heart rate, rate-pressure product and body temperature rose under both MDMA conditions against placebo, and lasted longer after the booster without a higher maximum. No systolic pressure above 180 mm Hg and no temperature above 40 degrees Celsius occurred in any participant.
key_findings.note: The values are in Supplementary Table S11 and Supplementary Figure S6, which were not read; the main text gives only this description.

key_findings.finding: Adverse effects were more common after both MDMA conditions than placebo and did not differ significantly between booster and single dose: complaint scores were 22 (SD 15) and 20 (SD 13) acutely against 4.4 (SD 5.3) for placebo, and 16 (SD 16) and 17 (SD 16) over days 0-3 against 7.7 (SD 13). The most frequent acute complaints were tiredness, lack of appetite, bruxism and headache; vomiting occurred in 3 of 23 (13%) in the booster condition and 2 (9%) in the single-dose condition. Somatic complaints faded by days 3 and 7 while psychological ones (rumination, fatigue, inner tension, restlessness) persisted.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, List of complaints rows; Results > Acute and subacute adverse effects, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Two of 25 participants (8%) left after one session, both women who had received the booster as their first MDMA experience: both had intense headache and nausea during the session and then weeks of anxiety, restlessness, tension or impaired concentration, one with reduced capacity for work improving over several months. One serious adverse event occurred, acute angle-closure glaucoma during a single-dose session in a participant later found to have narrow angles, with full recovery. Two men (9%) reported brief flashback-like recurrences of mild drug effects in the following days.
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute and subacute adverse effects, 3rd-4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: In exploratory, descriptive analyses complaint scores were nominally higher in women and in people under 65 kg, particularly after the booster, and vomiting occurred only in women, all weighing 57-63 kg; the authors note that sex and body weight could not be separated in this sample.
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute and subacute adverse effects, last sentence of the 1st paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Blinding largely failed: every participant identified the placebo condition correctly, 35 of 46 MDMA conditions (76%) were identified correctly immediately after the session and 40 of 46 (87%) by the end of the study.

Oxytocin and its carrier protein rose under both MDMA conditions against placebo, and were higher at 4 and 6 hours after the booster than after the single dose; the two measures correlated closely (r=0.86, p<0.0001).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the single-dose effect duration as 4.6 +/- 1.2 h while Table 1 gives 4.6 +/- 1.5 h for the same measure; the booster value (5.6 +/- 1.8 h) and the p value (0.001) agree.
reporting_issues.locator: Abstract; Table 1, 'Any drug effect' duration row
reporting_issues.consequence: The dispersion of the primary outcome differs between abstract and table; the table value should be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The pharmacokinetic table retains the two dropouts, giving n=25 for the booster condition and n=23 for the single dose, while every pharmacodynamic analysis uses the 23 completers; half-life and clearance rest on 15-16 profiles because the 9-hour observation was too short to characterize elimination in everyone, which the paper states.
reporting_issues.locator: Table 3 legend and n columns; Results > Pharmacokinetics
reporting_issues.consequence: The concentration comparison and the effect comparison are not made in exactly the same people, and the half-life figures rest on a subset; the ratio columns (n=23) are the ones to cite.

reporting_issues.issue: The peak subjective ratings against which acute tolerance is argued are already 83-87 out of 100, and the paper does not consider a ceiling on the scales as an alternative explanation for the unchanged peaks, although it names scale ceilings nowhere and applies the same reasoning to autonomic measures where no ceiling applies.
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim of acute tolerance should rest on the autonomic and duration data as much as on the subjective peaks, since a rating that is already near the top of its scale cannot rise further.

reporting_issues.issue: Most of the quantitative detail is in supplementary tables and figures that the main text only summarizes, including all autonomic values, the mood ratings, the hysteresis plot cited as evidence of acute tolerance, the complaint-symptom frequencies and the stratified analyses.
reporting_issues.locator: Results > Autonomic effects; Results > Acute subjective effects, last sentence; Results > Acute and subacute adverse effects
reporting_issues.consequence: Several statements in this card can be anchored only to the main text's wording, not to numbers; a second reader with the supplement should check the autonomic and hysteresis claims.

reporting_issues.issue: The two participants who dropped out, both of whom had the booster, are excluded from the within-person adverse-effect comparison, which then shows no significant difference between booster and single dose.
reporting_issues.locator: Results > Acute and subacute adverse effects, 3rd paragraph; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: The tolerability comparison is made among those who completed all three sessions; the two worst reactions, both in the booster condition, are reported separately and in words. The finding of no added harm from the booster should always be reported with those two cases.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1, the area under the effect curve for 'talkative' in the single-dose condition is 3.5 (SD 110), close to the placebo value of 4.7 (SD 22), although the same condition's peak rating is 23 (SD 19).
reporting_issues.consequence: The bidirectional scales subtract the area below baseline from the area above, so a large negative phase can cancel the peak; these area values are not comparable with the unidirectional ones and should not be quoted as a measure of effect size.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC13451183 (Translational Psychiatry 2026;16:402), read in the browser pane; Tables 1-3 render as text and were read in full, Figures 1-2 are images and no values were taken from them. The supplementary PDF was not read, and every statement that depends on it is marked in the card.
